messages.author: 91fe2d29e9575ba7
messages.subject: randow walk within locations
parts:
Dear all,

We have a dataset spanning about 20 years with data from about 1000 locations. Each location is sampled 6 times per year. A randow walk along year per location would be a good thing for this dataset. We sloved this by creating a new vector year2 = location * (nYear + 200) + year. So year2 looks like 1:20 for location 0,  201:220 for location 1, 401:420 for location 2, ... Then we added a f(year2, model = 'rw1') component to the model. Is this OK or is it rubbish? The example below seems to give reasonable results. Though the year2 effects seems to have some positive bias.

Best regards,

Thierry

library(INLA)
library(ggplot2)
set.seed(12345)
nLocation <- 20
nYear <- 20
nMonth <- 6
Intercept <- 3
Season <- 2
sdYear <- 0.1
sdTrend <- 0.05
sdLocation <- 3
rho <- 0.5
burnin <- 50
probMissing <- 0.2

dataset <- expand.grid(year = seq_len(nYear), month = seq_len(nMonth), location = seq_len(nLocation))
dataset$Fixed <- Intercept + Season * cos(pi * (dataset$month - round(mean(dataset$month))) / nMonth)
Random <- matrix(rnorm(nLocation, mean = 0, sd = sdLocation), ncol = nYear + burnin, nrow = nLocation)

Error <- matrix(rnorm((nYear + burnin) * nLocation, mean = 0, sd = sdYear), ncol = nYear + burnin)
for(i in tail(seq_len(nYear + burnin), -1)){
  Random[, i] <- rho * Random[, i - 1] + Error[, i]
}
Random <- Random[, -seq_len(burnin)]
dataset$Random <- apply(dataset[, c("location", "year")], 1, function(x){
  Random[x["location"], x["year"]]
})
dataset$Random <- dataset$Random + rnorm(nLocation, mean = 0, sd = sdTrend)[dataset$location] * dataset$year
dataset$y <- rpois(nrow(dataset), lambda = exp(dataset$Fixed + dataset$Random))
dataset$y0 <- dataset$y
dataset$y[rbinom(nrow(dataset), prob = probMissing, size = 1) == 1] <- NA
ggplot(subset(dataset, !is.na(y)), aes(x = year, y = location)) + geom_point() + facet_wrap(~month)
ggplot(dataset, aes(x = year, y = y0, colour = factor(month))) + geom_line() + facet_wrap(~location, scales = "free_y")


dataset$year2 <- with(dataset, location * (nYear + 200) + year)
link <- rep(NA, nrow(dataset))
link[is.na(dataset$y)] <- 1
model3 <- inla(y ~ factor(month) + f(year2, model = "rw1"), family = "poisson", data = dataset, control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE, link = link))
plot(model3)
test <- merge(dataset, model3$summary.random$year2, by.x = "year2", by.y = "ID")
colnames(test)[11:13] <- c("LCL", "Median", "UCL")
ggplot(test, aes(x = year, y = Random)) + geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = LCL, ymax = UCL), alpha = 0.1, fill = "blue") + geom_line(aes(y = mean), colour = "blue") + geom_line() + facet_wrap(~location, scales = "free_y")

On 08/03/13 10:00, thierry....@gmail.com wrote:
> Dear all,
>
> We have a dataset spanning about 20 years with data from about 1000
> locations. Each location is sampled 6 times per year. A randow walk
> along year per location would be a good thing for this dataset. We
> sloved this by creating a new vector year2 = location * (nYear + 200)
> + year. So year2 looks like 1:20 for location 0, 201:220 for location
> 1, 401:420 for location 2, ... Then we added a f(year2, model = 'rw1')
> component to the model. Is this OK or is it rubbish? The example below
> seems to give reasonable results. Though the year2 effects seems to
> have some positive bias.

Hi, it should be a rough approximation of independent realisations for
each location, since you have relatively long gaps in between the
segments you use, but the correct way to do that is to use "replicate"
in the f() specifications, and use 1:20 for every location in "year2".
That will also reduce the size of your model drastically.

Finn

parts: On 08/03/13 10:00, thierry....@gmail.com wrote:

> walk along year per location would be a good thing for this dataset.
> We sloved this by creating a new vector year2 = location * (nYear +
> 200) + year. So year2 looks like 1:20 for location 0, 201:220 for
> location 1, 401:420 for location 2, ... Then we added a f(year2, model
> = 'rw1') component to the model. Is this OK or is it rubbish? The
> example below seems to give reasonable results. Though the year2
> effects seems to have some positive bias.

Something like this should do the trick:

year2 = rep(1:20, times=nLocations)
repl = rep(1:nLocations, each=nYear)
f(year2, model="rw1", replicate=repl)

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] randow walk within locations
parts:
On 08/03/13 10:14, Finn Lindgren wrote:
> Though the year2 effects seems to have some positive bias.

Bear in mind that the rw1 model by default has a sum-to-zero constraint,
which I suspect will make your method behave strangely, partly because
you're not attaching any data to most of the values in the model. The
"replicate" method would instead applies the sum-to-zero constraint on
each replication, and only has the 20 years for each location, giving
you a lot more control over the model, if for example you want to
include another part of the full model to model the mean values at each
location.

Finn

>
> Something like this should do the trick:
>
> year2 = rep(1:20, times=nLocations)
> repl = rep(1:nLocations, each=nYear)
> f(year2, model="rw1", replicate=repl)

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] randow walk within locations
parts:
On 08/03/13 10:14, Finn Lindgren wrote:
>

> Something like this should do the trick:
>
> year2 = rep(1:20, times=nLocations)
> repl = rep(1:nLocations, each=nYear)
> f(year2, model="rw1", replicate=repl)

I missed the "sampled 6 times per year" part. That requires modifying
both rep statements slightly, but since the principle is the same but
simpler than you original "hack", you should be able to work out the
details. Send me an email otherwise...

Finn

parts:
Dear Finn,

Thanks a lot for your feedback. I went for the solution below. It's a
pitty that the replicate argument does not takes factors.

inla(y ~ factor(month) + f(year, model = "rw1", replicate = location) +
f(location, model = "iid"), family = "poisson", data = dataset,
control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE, link = link))

Best regards,

Thierry
